title: Battery EPR Desk for E-Mobility Importers
one_liner: A retainer compliance service that registers, reports and budgets for battery EPR on behalf of small e-bike, scooter and power-station brands.
customer: E-bike, e-scooter, power-station and power-tool brand owners and importers of record selling into California and other battery-EPR states, typically $2-100M revenue with no regulatory staff.
problem: California signed SB 501 on Sept 20, 2026, creating medium-format battery EPR with a 60% recycling-efficiency floor. Thousands of small importers and marketplace sellers cannot parse who counts as the producer, how to pick or join a PRO, or what to report. Their packs also drive facility fires.
solution: Producer determination, PRO registration, automated unit and weight reporting from Shopify and Amazon data, fee budgeting, labeling artwork, take-back partnering, and a battery data sheet (chemistry, mass, removability). Recyclers want that sheet, and the evidence pack satisfies audits.
why_now: SB 501 was signed days ago, and California signed it while vetoing other bills. Existing state battery laws and the 74 catastrophic facility fires this year mean regulators and marketplaces will demand proof.
revenue_model: $6-24K per year retainer, plus 5-10% markup on pass-through PRO fees and take-back costs.
non_obvious_insight: The buyer is not the famous brand but 3,000 small importers who cannot read statute. Becoming the compliance layer that marketplaces reference flips the distribution problem.
first_30_days: Build an 'Am I a producer?' quiz. Scrape marketplaces for e-mobility brands selling into California and email 300. Sign 10 for a $1.5K registration audit. Approach one marketplace's compliance team.

title: Manufactured-Home Replacement With Salvage Financing
angle: Pairing 2: Construction/housing shortage/trades labor/home services x Waste/recycling/circular economy/critical minerals/materials
one_liner: A turnkey 'old home out, new home in' program for manufactured-home communities: hazmat survey, salvage and teardown of pre-1976 units, pad prep, then set-and-hookup crews for new factory-built homes, with scrap and reuse value helping finance the job.
customer: Manufactured-home community owners and resident-owned communities replacing derelict units, state and nonprofit replacement programs, and chattel lenders.
problem: Old manufactured homes are a huge stock of unsubsidized affordable housing, but many are at end of life. Removing one costs thousands (asbestos survey, hazmat, disposal) and takes weeks. Even as factory-built homes get cheaper, foundations, utility hookups, set crews and local financing stay local and human. The July 2026 ROAD to Housing Act killed the steel chassis rule (about $10K or 10% of unit cost), but HUD has yet to publish the new standards.
solution: A fixed-price 'decommission and pad-ready in 10 days' package: survey, harvest steel frame, axles, aluminum, copper and appliances, and route scrap and hazmat properly. Then a set-and-hookup crew for the new home, plus a lender referral and a trade-in credit that offsets the down payment. Park owners buy the program to upgrade lots.
why_now: ROAD to Housing Act (Jul 11, 2026) makes factory-built housing cheaper and HUD's standards are imminent. Tariffs raise steel and material costs, site-crew scarcity is acute, and PE-owned parks want faster unit turnover.
revenue_model: Fixed fee of roughly $6-12K per replacement (salvage revenue offsets perhaps a fifth to a third of removal cost); lender and dealer referral fees; set-crew margin later.
non_obvious_insight: The replacement bottleneck is not the factory but the exit of the old unit. Salvage and hazmat know-how turn a cost into a program, and a trade-in credit is what makes chattel financing pencil for the resident.
first_30_days: Approach 5 park owners or resident-owned co-ops with 5-20 derelict homes each. Price a pilot batch of 10 homes. Run asbestos surveys, take scrap to yards and document real per-home cost and cycle time. Use the results to sign the first paid batch and a lender partner.

title: Fast-Pay Administrator for Funded Home Repair
one_liner: Run the paperwork and pay small contractors in days on grant- and program-funded repairs (weatherization, aging-in-place, municipal repair programs) where waitlists exist because few pros will bid.
customer: Nonprofits, community action agencies, Area Agencies on Aging, housing authorities and municipal home-repair programs with budgets but weak execution capacity.
problem: Programs have money but not throughput: jobs are small ($2-15K), paperwork-heavy (income verification, lead-safe rules, photos, inspections) and reimbursed in 30-90 days. Good contractors are too busy for low-margin, slow-pay work. The median home is 44 years old, repair-over-replace is at 62%, and homeowners cannot get quotes.
solution: Act as general contractor of record plus payment desk: take the program's approved scope, match it to vetted small pros, run documentation and inspections in a phone workflow, pay the pro in 5-7 days by fronting cash, and bill the agency with audit-ready files. The agency's program-delivery budget line pays the admin fee.
why_now: Aging housing stock and record remodeling spend ($524B) mean small pros have plenty of alternatives to slow-pay work. Vision and document models make photo-based compliance cheap. Slower remodeling growth (about 1.6% by year-end) should free some pro capacity for steady program work.
revenue_model: 12-18% admin fee on job value paid by the agency, plus a 1-2% factoring spread on advances.
non_obvious_insight: In public repair programs the scarce input is neither money nor eligible homeowners, it is good contractors' willingness to endure paperwork and slow pay. Fast payment plus document automation is the moat, and the customer already has a budget line for program delivery.
first_30_days: Approach five agencies with waitlists in one state. Offer a 10-job cost-plus pilot. Recruit 10 small pros on a 7-day-pay promise. Open a $75K working-capital line and run documentation through simple phone forms.

title: Heat and Smoke Stop-Day Kit for Outdoor Crews
one_liner: Text-message heat and smoke compliance for small outdoor employers, sold through comp carriers and PEOs, with parametric stop-day cover to follow.
customer: Workers' comp carriers and PEOs serving small landscapers, roofers, framers and farms in California, Washington and Oregon (later AZ, TX, CO), plus general contractors that need subs' plans.
problem: OSHA's federal heat rule has slipped (supplemental proposal Dec 2026, final Oct 2027), but California, Washington and Oregon already bind employers. Small crews have no written plan, acclimatization tracking or go/no-go rule. Heat and smoke stop-work days hurt small-contractor cash flow, and business-interruption cover for them is barely productized.
solution: Phase one is a text-message-first kit: site-level heat and air-quality alerts, a state-specific written plan, water, shade and break logs, acclimatization schedules and audit exports. Phase two adds parametric stop-day cover through an MGA partner, with WBGT or AQI triggers.
why_now: The summer 2026 shock and state rules make compliance urgent, while federal delay pushes pressure onto carriers and GCs.
revenue_model: $39-99 per crew per month, or per-employee fees from carriers and PEOs for loss control, plus parametric premium margin later.
non_obvious_insight: Demand does not depend on OSHA. States, general-contractor prequalification and comp-carrier loss control drive it.
first_30_days: Pitch two comp-carrier loss-control teams and a landscaping association. Run a 20-crew pilot with the plan generator and alerts.

title: Payroll-Deducted Paylater Refinance for Factory Workers
one_liner: Consolidate minimum-wage workers' paylater and online loans into one payroll-deducted instalment, sold to the employer as retention.
customer: Indonesian manufacturers and retailers with 1,000+ minimum-wage staff, especially in Java's industrial belts; employers pay a fee and a partner lender funds.
problem: Paylater financing reached Rp43.28T in May and online lending Rp100.69T, and defaults are rising among minimum-wage workers. Collection harassment causes absenteeism and turnover.
solution: Consolidate a worker's paylater and pinjol debts into one lower-rate loan repaid via payroll, funded by a licensed multifinance or bank partner. The wedge is three factories in Bekasi and Karawang.
why_now: OJK scrutiny is rising and the 2026 macro squeeze is pushing defaults up.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus lender spread share, and an employer fee of Rp10-15k per worker per month.
non_obvious_insight: The paylater trap is an HR problem before it is a credit problem, and the employer is the only party with payroll access and a reason to care.
first_30_days: Interview HR heads at three factories and pilot with 200 workers using a partner lender.

title: Part-Time Seats: Districts Sell Classes to Homeschoolers
one_liner: Software and a playbook that lets shrinking districts enroll homeschoolers and microschoolers a la carte and capture per-pupil funding they are now losing.
customer: Declining-enrollment suburban and rural districts and small charters (superintendents, budget directors) in states that allow part-time or shared-time enrollment.
problem: K-12 enrollment fell from 50.8M to 49.4M (2019-24) and is projected at 46.9M by 2031, with more than 1,000 closures in 2025-26. Districts treat homeschool and microschool families as lost. Yet only about 10% of homeschool families do it K-12 exclusively and 30% do it for 1-2 years (lower-confidence data), so many want labs, band, AP, CTE shops and sports.
solution: A part-time enrollment desk: a catalog of under-filled classes (chem lab, band, welding shop, AP), a family portal for enrollment, records, immunization and attendance, FTE and funding counting per state rules, a la carte billing, and transcript conversion for re-entry. The pitch is that a marginal seat in an empty class costs nearly nothing.
why_now: The enrollment cliff has become a budget crisis. Homeschool ESA families are second-class (Texas homeschoolers get $2,000 against $10,474 for private-school kids), and over 70% of homeschoolers in non-ESA states say they would take public funds. Scholarship-credit and ESA dollars from 2027 can pay for a la carte seats.
revenue_model: $8-25k per year SaaS per district, or a per-enrollment fee of $50-150, or a 5-10% share of incremental revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Districts fight choice by trying to keep full-time kids, but the untapped resource is empty seats in existing classes. Transient and hybrid families are exactly the buyers, and part-time enrollment doubles as a re-entry ramp that brings kids back.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a clear part-time or shared-time statute. Recruit 2 budget-stressed districts for a free pilot. Publish the seat catalog to local homeschool groups. Measure seats sold for the January semester and funding captured.

title: Last Day Co: Small Business Wind-Down
one_liner: A flat-fee retirement service for owners who do not want to sell, just stop: legal wind-down, lease exit, records custody, customer-list handoff and a proper last day.
customer: Retiring owners of solo and micro businesses with $100k to $2M in revenue. Start with regulated solo practices (therapists, small medical or dental practices, solo attorneys, CPAs) where closing duties create urgency, then salons, restaurants and contractors.
problem: McKinsey estimates baby boomers run as many as 6M small and midsize US businesses, with roughly 2.3M to 3M expected to transition ownership this decade, yet only about 54% of owners have a succession plan and about a third of owners over 50 say they cannot find a buyer. Brokers are paid only on sales and skip tiny firms, so most simply shut. That leaves leases, personal guarantees, client records, final payroll and taxes, licenses and customers stranded.
solution: A productized 90-day closure: state and local filings and final taxes through a partner CPA, lease exit negotiation (buyout or assignment, limiting the personal guarantee), equipment and inventory liquidation, and a records-custody service where Last Day Co acts as professional custodian for 7 to 10 years with client notice and a release process. It also brokers the customer list or goodwill to a vetted local competitor, with a fee to the owner. It closes with a last-day package: customer letter, farewell event, staff reference packets.
why_now: Boomers are now roughly 62 to 80, so closures are rising toward the McKinsey-projected peak. LLMs make state-specific closure checklists, notices and letters cheap to produce accurately. Remote records custody removes the need for a physical archive.
revenue_model: A $2,500 to $9,000 flat wind-down fee. Records custody at $25 to $75 per month or a prepaid $1,500 for 7 years. A goodwill-handoff success fee of 10% to 20% of what the acquirer pays. A 10% to 15% liquidation commission.
non_obvious_insight: Brokers sell, and nobody closes. Most owners do not want a sale process, they want to stop, so the real product is permission and completion with liability handled. Custodianship for regulated practices is near-zero-churn recurring revenue, and the customer list is the only asset that survives a closure, so a warm handoff to a neighboring competitor is where the money is.
first_30_days: Pick solo therapists and solo attorneys in one state. With a local attorney and CPA, write the state-specific 'professional will and closure' playbook. Sell the $299 professional will plus closure plan through the state association newsletter and LinkedIn. Do three discounted pilot closures end to end, build a list of local acquirers for goodwill handoffs, and document each step as a repeatable checklist.

title: Sewage Nielsen: Wastewater Consumption Index
one_liner: Weekly per-capita consumption of alcohol, nicotine, cannabis and caffeine, measured from metabolites in city wastewater and sold to alt-data funds and regulators as a Nielsen for vices.
customer: Alt-data-buying hedge funds and long-only consumer analysts covering alcohol, tobacco and nicotine pouches, cannabis and energy drinks. Secondary: state cannabis and tax regulators who want to size legal versus illicit share, and cannabis operators or beverage companies buying custom market studies.
problem: Investors debating whether GLP-1 drugs and Gen Z are actually cutting alcohol, or whether nicotine pouches and cannabis are cannibalizing other products, rely on lagging, self-reported or scanner data. Those sources miss the illicit, gray-market, direct-to-consumer and cash segments. Regulators cannot measure the illicit cannabis share either.
solution: Composite-sample assays at 15-25 wastewater treatment plants across major metros, run weekly by a partner analytical lab (LC-MS/MS). Measure alcohol (ethyl sulfate), nicotine (cotinine), cannabis (THC-COOH) and caffeine metabolites. Normalize with population markers and flow to get per-capita consumption estimates. Only report at sewersheds serving 50k+ people, which handles privacy. Deliver as a weekly index via API and CSV with methodology notes. Sell a historical series built from archived samples.
why_now: The GLP-1 alcohol-reduction debate is a live equity question. Nicotine pouches and cannabis regulation are moving fast. Wastewater programs built with pandemic-era public health funding are shrinking or uncertain, which leaves utilities, university labs, sampling gear and freezer archives idle and open to co-funding. Alt-data budgets keep growing and funds want signals with no retail-panel bias.
revenue_model: Alt-data subscription of roughly 60-250k USD per year per fund, with tiered metro coverage. Government and regulator contracts (illicit-market sizing). Custom brand or category studies of 25-100k USD. Later, per-sewershed expansions paid by cities as a public-health co-benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Sewage is the only consumption panel that cannot be gamed, self-reported or missed by scanner data, because it captures what people actually consume regardless of channel. The science has been used by European drug-monitoring networks for 15 years, but nobody has packaged it as a consumer-sector economic indicator. Pandemic-era freezer archives of stored samples let you sell a multi-year backtestable history on day one, which is the thing quant buyers require before they will pay.
first_30_days: Partner with a university lab that already has validated LC-MS/MS methods for these metabolites and old COVID-monitoring relationships with treatment plants. Sign MOUs with 3-5 plants. Run assays on archived samples to build a 2021-2025 backtest series for those sewersheds. Pitch 15 alt-data funds and data-aggregator marketplaces with the backtest chart of one hook (for example alcohol per-capita against local retail sales). Launch a pilot at 5 sewersheds with 2-3 design-partner funds paying pilot fees. Note that the plan depends on plant access agreements and lab throughput.

title: IEP-Ready Adaptive Hardware, Printed to Order
one_liner: A micro-manufacturer that acts as the approved vendor for special-education adaptive hardware, starting with custom AAC keyguards for tablets and expanding to OT-prescribed grips, switch mounts and positioning aids.
customer: School district special-ed and assistive-technology coordinators, school SLPs and OTs, and private pediatric therapy clinics, paid through district purchase orders funded by IEP obligations.
problem: Free keyguard designs exist, and Etsy sellers make standard ones. But an SLP has no time to print, a district can't pay an Etsy seller by purchase order, and a custom AAC grid on a specific tablet and case needs an exact fit. Legally required AT then arrives weeks late. Every tablet or case refresh orphans last year's keyguards.
solution: A catalog and a 48-hour custom service. The SLP uploads a screenshot of the AAC layout and the tablet and case model. We return a fit-verified keyguard with an IEP-friendly quote and invoice. Then expand to OT-prescribed items (pencil grips, adaptive handles, switch and tablet mounts, tactile schedule boards) using a clinician-approved parametric library. Paperwork arrives ready for the file: W-9, liability insurance, net-30 terms and cooperative-purchasing listings.
why_now: Consumer-grade printing is now reliable enough for small runs of durable parts. Tablet-based AAC is now standard practice, and app grid layouts are standardized enough to parametrize. Districts are under pressure to meet AT obligations with tight budgets. Open-source designs prove the demand but leave the procurement gap wide open.
revenue_model: Per item ($35 to $95 for keyguards; $10 to $150 for other adaptive items), plus an annual district 'AT Bench' subscription ($3k to $8k covering a set number of custom items and a design consult).
non_obvious_insight: The scarce thing isn't the printing or even the design, since clinicians will share designs for free. It's the procurement wrapper: being a vendor a district can legally and easily pay. Whoever holds 'approved vendor' status with a few purchasing cooperatives gets pulled into every district's AT budget. Print cost is $4 against a $80 to $150 price because the customer is paying for zero-friction compliance and clinical fit.
first_30_days: Take the open-source keyguard parametric files and verify fit against the five most common tablet and case combinations. Post in SLP and AT groups: 'send a screenshot of your layout, first keyguard at cost, PO accepted.' Complete vendor registration with two districts and apply to one purchasing cooperative. Target 15 paid orders and one district relationship.

title: Program Survival Analytics for Regional Universities
one_liner: A subscription that tells provosts which degree programs will fail the new federal earnings tests and loan-cap economics as AI hollows out their feeder occupations, with a redesign playbook.
customer: Provosts, institutional research offices and deans at regional universities, master's-heavy colleges and online providers ($20-60k a year), plus state systems.
problem: As I understand the 2025 budget law (verify specifics), programs whose graduates don't out-earn benchmarks can lose loan eligibility, and Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers with new caps from July 2026. Graduate programs in cognitive fields (analytics, MBA, MS CS, communications) rely on borrowing, while entry-level demand is falling (NY Fed: 42% recent-grad underemployment). Institutions see it only when enrollment drops.
solution: A program-level model combining College Scorecard earnings, occupation-level job-posting trends, AI-exposure scores and enrollment and borrowing data. It delivers early-warning flags, a scenario tool, recommended pivots (in-degree apprenticeships, short credentials, employer co-design) backed by real employer demand signals, and board-ready compliance reporting.
why_now: The new loan and accountability rules began July 2026, the AI-driven junior hiring freeze is measurable (Stanford: 19% gap for ages 22-25), and university budgets are tight.
revenue_model: Annual licence of $20-60k, program-redesign consulting and state-system contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Universities already face compliance deadlines, but nobody has tied AI exposure to the earnings-test math. A federal deadline creates budget urgency that 'future of work' advice never gets. The first programs to fail are likely master's degrees in cognitive fields.
first_30_days: Build the model from public Scorecard data for ~200 institutions as a proof. Generate 'programs at risk' reports for 20 target universities' master's programs and email institutional-research directors and provosts. Sell three $7.5k pilot diagnostics.

title: Lot-Level Reagent Reliability Oracle for Buyer Agents
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Biotech tools / synbio / lab automation
one_liner: A neutral, pooled 'Carfax for reagent lots' that tells human and agent buyers whether this specific lot of serum, Matrigel, antibody or PBMC has worked in other labs before they order it.
customer: Cell-culture, organoid and iPSC labs at startups, CROs and universities. API customers are lab-procurement and ELN agents that place orders. Buyers are lab managers and platform teams with a per-lab subscription.
problem: Lot-to-lot variability is the tribal knowledge of biology. Matrigel has about 1,800 proteins and is specified only as 8-22 mg/mL, and a cross-site study found 2,188 differentially expressed genes by day 84. Labs test-and-reserve serum lots and trade warnings on Slack. Certificates of analysis do not predict downstream performance. Autonomous purchasing and ELN agents will happily reorder the cheapest 'equivalent' lot with no lore, and agents repeating analyses already vary stochastically. Pharma cannot pool this data across competitors.
solution: An opt-in ELN/LIMS plug-in and Slack bot logs only lot number, cell line or assay type and a coarse outcome flag (grew, differentiated, failed QC). It pools this anonymized across subscribers into a lot-performance ledger. Humans and agents query it by MCP or API before ordering ('lot X failed iPSC-organoid differentiation in 4 of 9 labs') and get alerts if a lot already in their freezer turns bad. The service also brokers lot reservations and lot swaps between labs.
why_now: Organoids and NAMs are being pushed by the FDA's September 21, 2026 rule swapping 'animal tests' for 'nonclinical tests' that must be 'adequately validated', which makes reagent consistency a validation problem. Labs are also starting to let agents place orders, and 2026 procurement agents have price and spec data but no lab lore.
revenue_model: Lab subscription ($199-499/month); per-query API fees for procurement agents; pharma/CRO enterprise tier with private cohorts and lot-reservation brokerage (commission on brokered inventory). Vendors cannot pay for scores, but can buy anonymized post-market performance reports.
non_obvious_insight: The scarcest input for an autonomous purchasing agent is not price or spec but lab lore, and lot performance is a free by-product of ELN activity that nobody captures. A neutral aggregator can pool what competing pharmas never will because only lot-level flags leave the lab.
first_30_days: Start with one painful category, fetal bovine serum plus Matrigel/BME, in one community (an organoid or iPSC Slack/Discord group). Have 20 labs log lot outcomes through a form or Slack bot, and publish a weekly 'lot alert' newsletter. Convert the 5 most active labs to a paid tier with private alerts. Add the ELN plug-in only after the data proves useful.

title: Playable-Until Guarantees for Online Games
one_liner: Sell publishers a pre-funded shutdown trust plus an escrowed server kit, so a dated playability guarantee becomes a selling point for $70-80 online games instead of a legal risk.
customer: Indie and mid-size publishers (10-300 staff) of co-op and live-service titles on Steam and console, and premium online games priced at $70-80.
problem: Publishers treat any end-of-life promise as a liability admission, so buyers get none. Anthem shut down on 2026-01-12, and of 738 tracked shutdown games 68% are unplayable or at risk. The EU Commission declined a mandatory rule on 2026-06-16 but wants a voluntary code by end of 2026. UFC-Que Choisir sued Ubisoft over The Crew, and a suit against Sony followed in Aug 2026.
solution: A 'Last Light' package with three parts. (1) Escrow of a server-emulator kit, builds and docs, verified by a clean-room restore drill we run. (2) A small per-title trust funded at launch (1-2% of gross) that pays a hosting partner to keep a minimal community server up for N years. (3) A store-page badge with a date, plus a public verification page. If a sunset trigger fires, the kit is released to the community.
why_now: The EU voluntary code of conduct due by end of 2026 will set a de facto standard that needs an auditor. The Stop Killing Games petition has 1.29M verified signers, a ready-made audience. $70-80 pricing needs a value story, and the Ubisoft and Sony suits show the cost of staying silent.
revenue_model: Certification and restore-drill fee of $8-40k per title, 15-20% admin retention on trust contributions, and $3-5k annual re-certification.
non_obvious_insight: A bounded, dated, funded promise caps liability, while silence leaves it open-ended and now litigated. Most online games reduce to stateless auth and matchmaking, so the guarantee is cheap to keep. Publishers also get a marketing asset that the Stop Killing Games community will actively promote.
first_30_days: Recruit volunteer engineers from the Stop Killing Games community to draft a reference escrow spec. Pitch 30 indie co-op publishers with launches in the next 12 months. Run a free restore drill on one willing title and publish it as a case study. Presell 3 pilots at $5-8k, and get a hosting-partner letter of intent and a lawyer-reviewed template.

title: Guardrail Gateway for Law-Firm AI Agents
one_liner: A policy proxy between AI agents and practice-management, billing and trust-accounting systems that enforces ethics rules (trust funds, conflicts, confidentiality) and logs every action for the bar and the insurer.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys), the exact segment adopting MCP connectors. Distribution partners are practice-management vendors and malpractice carriers that want to underwrite agent use.
problem: 8am's MyCase MCP connector exposes 73 actions across cases, billing and intake, and 60+ firms adopted it in month one. An agent that can write to billing and trust ledgers can commingle funds, send a privileged detail to the wrong client or email a client without review. Those are disciplinary and malpractice events that no hallucination checker prevents, and solo lawyers have no IT staff, policy or audit trail.
solution: An MCP gateway between Claude, ChatGPT or a 'Firm Agent' and Clio, MyCase and LawPay. Rules block any write touching the trust account without attorney approval by SMS, enforce ethical walls between matters, redact privileged content going to non-approved models, hold outbound client communications for review and rate-limit actions. Every call goes into a tamper-evident log, and a monthly 'agent audit' PDF answers the insurer questionnaire.
why_now: 8am launched its MCP integration in Sep 2026 and says nearly all of its new Firm Agent features already work via MCP, so law-practice data is flowing to third-party agents for the first time. ABA Formal Opinion 512 (2024) on generative-AI ethics gives the duties a written source (background, verify).
revenue_model: $79-199/firm/month, carrier-sponsored programs at $10-20 per insured firm per month, and white-label licensing to practice-management vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The risk from agents is authority (moving money and information), not wrong words. Legal ethics rules are crisp about authority (trust accounting, confidentiality, conflicts), so they compile into policy, unlike 'accuracy'. Distribution will run through practice-management marketplaces, not law-firm websites.
first_30_days: Build the gateway for one platform (Clio or MyCase MCP) with six rules. Recruit 10 small firms through user groups and run it free as a 30-day 'agent audit' that shows near-misses, then convert at $99/month. Take the audit output to two state-bar-affiliated malpractice carriers.

title: Guaranteed Midday Walker as Apartment Amenity
one_liner: Sell apartment operators a fixed on-site walker window as a renewal and lease-up amenity, with residents paying a discounted per-walk fee and the building paying a retainer.
customer: Owners and property managers of 150 to 500 unit multifamily buildings in dense metros, paying a monthly retainer. Residents are the secondary payers.
problem: A solo walker loses 35 to 45 percent of the paid day to driving between homes, parking, and building lobbies. Buildings, meanwhile, pay quietly for dogs: barking and noise complaints, damage from anxious dogs, waste on the property, and hidden-dog lease violations. Pet owners renew at higher rates than other tenants, but it is hard to monetize them with pet rent, especially where fees are capped or scrutinized.
solution: A walker holds fixed weekday windows (for example 11am to 2pm and 5 to 7pm) in the building, using the fob and package room. Residents book by QR code or text, and the walker walks compatible dogs from nearby floors in groups of 3 to 4 (dog compatibility is something a walker learns quickly), with a lobby handoff. Yield per hour roughly doubles or triples versus door-to-door, so residents pay about $12 to $15 per walk instead of $25 to $30. The building gets a monthly report on walks completed, incidents, and waste-bag use, plus marketing copy ('guaranteed midday walk') for lease-up and renewals. I could not confirm in this session whether a comparable product already operates at scale, so check competitors first.
why_now: Return-to-office mandates put more dogs alone midday. Big multifamily supply waves in many metros mean operators compete on concessions and retention, and are shifting amenity spend from gyms to services. Pet-fee restrictions in some states and cities push operators to bundle services instead of charging rent. Simple text-and-QR booking removes the back-office cost that used to make this unprofitable.
revenue_model: Building retainer of roughly $1,500 to $3,000 a month for guaranteed windows, plus resident per-walk fees of $12 to $15, plus optional add-ons (waste station servicing, dog-friendly move-in tours). Expand by selling to regional operators as a portfolio amenity program.
non_obvious_insight: The walker's real margin killer is geography, not demand. A walker's hourly income is decided by drive time and cancellations, so the fix is to put demand where the walker already is. What operators really buy is not walks, it is fewer noise complaints and higher pet-owner renewals, so price it against retention, not against Rover.
first_30_days: Start with a building where you already walk two or three dogs. Ask those residents to introduce you to the community manager. Pitch a 60-day pilot at about $750 a month with walk windows and a resident-sign-up QR poster. Measure sign-ups and complaints, then take the numbers to two more buildings in the same operator or neighborhood.

title: Independent Verifier for LLM Inference Endpoints
one_liner: Continuous black-box testing that proves an API endpoint is serving the advertised model at the advertised precision, with a price-per-verified-quality index.
customer: AI-native companies and enterprises spending $50k+ per month on inference through routers, resellers and open-weights hosts, their procurement teams, and providers who want a 'Verified' badge.
problem: Endpoints can silently swap models, quantise or truncate context. Research on model substitution in LLM APIs (including an IRIS audit paper in July 2026) shows the problem is real, and a frontier lab's April 2026 postmortem acknowledged unadvertised changes that degraded output for weeks. No standard binds a response to a provider and model, so buyers cannot audit.
solution: Always-on probes from multiple regions using statistical fingerprints, random-string tests, tool-call accuracy and long-context recall. Alert on drift, publish a procurement dashboard of verified quality per dollar and a quarterly integrity leaderboard, and issue a 'Verified Endpoint' badge and SLA to providers.
why_now: Router and reseller markets exploded in 2025-26, margin pressure encourages silent quantisation, and agent workloads make small quality cuts expensive at scale. Fresh research gives credible detection methods.
revenue_model: $1-10k per month per buyer (scaled to spend), a share of verified savings, and $5-25k provider certification fees.
non_obvious_insight: This is a market for lemons. A 20% quality cut is invisible per request but material in aggregate, and the auditor's edge is statistical sampling at scale, not access to the provider.
first_30_days: Open-source the probe kit and publish a leaderboard across 30 endpoints serving the same open-weights model. Get five agent startups to run it, then convert to paid monitoring.

title: Home-Readiness Crews for Hospital-at-Home Programs
one_liner: On-call crews that make a patient's home hospital-ready in hours and provide a non-clinical overnight presence for the first 72 hours.
customer: Hospital-at-Home program directors at health systems, and Medicare Advantage plans and ACOs that fund them.
problem: Extending the waiver lets programs scale, but many referred patients get screened out because of clutter, stairs, pets, bad Wi-Fi or power, no bedside space, or no adult present overnight. Every screen-out is a lost admission that would have replaced $2,500+ inpatient days. No one owns the home itself.
solution: A van and two-person crew does a rapid home assessment (power, connectivity via hotspot or eSIM, safe path, bedside setup, hazard removal, DME handoff). A vetted sitter provides overnight presence and escalates to the nurse line, and the crew resets the home at discharge. An address-based readiness score pre-screens referrals before the ED sends them.
why_now: The Hospital-at-Home waiver was extended five years, to Sep 30, 2030, so systems are committing capital and hiring. 80+ growth and 90% occupancy in senior housing mean more frail patients whose homes are the constraint.
revenue_model: Per-episode fee of $350-900 plus monthly retainers for guaranteed response, and a software license for the readiness score.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource isn't clinicians or tech; it's a safe physical environment and a body in the room at 3 am. Whoever solves 'make the home hospital-grade' raises hospital-at-home conversion rates, which is what programs are judged on.
first_30_days: Pitch three hospital-at-home directors and offer a pilot at cost on 20 episodes, using existing local caregiver and sitter pools. Track screen-out conversion and cost per episode.

title: Integrity Desk for Grant Applications
one_liner: Cross-funder screening that catches AI-mass-produced applications, recycled proposals and forged partner letters before reviewers waste time.
customer: Community foundations, corporate giving programmes, state and regional economic-development agencies and accelerators, reached through grant-management platforms such as Submittable and Foundant.
problem: NIH capped principal investigators at six applications a year (effective 25 Sep 2025) after one applicant filed 40+ apparently AI-generated applications, and it says AI-developed proposals are not original work. Funders elsewhere see multiples of prior volume. Letters of support and partner commitments are the easiest thing to fabricate, and the same proposal is shopped to many funders.
solution: A plug-in and API for grant portals. It scores text reuse and AI boilerplate across applicants (including anonymised cross-funder fingerprints) and verifies claims and citations. It automatically calls back signatories of support letters for signed confirmation, checks entity registrations, tax status and beneficial owners, and keeps a shared duplicate-application registry across member funders.
why_now: LLMs drove the volume flood that prompted NIH's 2025 policy. Foundation staffing is thin, and federal and state scrutiny of grant fraud is rising.
revenue_model: $5-25k per cycle for foundations, $0.50-5 per application via portal partners, and registry membership for funders.
non_obvious_insight: This is the cURL lesson. When the cost of submission falls to zero, the reviewer's attention is the scarce resource. The winning move is not detecting AI text, which is unreliable, but verifying checkable third-party facts, like a partner's confirmation call, that AI cannot fake for free.
first_30_days: Run free pilot scans on last cycle's applications for three community foundations through regional grantmaker associations. Publish anonymised findings such as the share of applications with heavy text overlap. Pitch one grant-software vendor for a plug-in partnership.

title: Guest-Funded Wildfire Hardening for Vacation Rentals
angle: Pairing 1: Climate adaptation x Travel/hospitality (insurance retreat and short-term rentals)
one_liner: An opt-in per-night 'fire-safe stay' fee that lets guests pay down the ember-proofing of the vacation homes they rent, unlocking insurance credits and renewals for owners who cannot afford the retrofit.
customer: Owners and property managers of vacation rentals and cabins in wildfire-exposed resort towns (Lake Tahoe/Truckee, Big Bear, Mammoth, Idyllwild, Estes Park, Ruidoso, Gatlinburg, Sunriver) facing nonrenewals or multiples of prior premiums. Insurers writing in distressed ZIPs are a secondary payer for leads.
problem: Retrofit baselines run $8K-25K while insurer discounts are only 5-35%, so owners cannot front the cash and the credit is unclaimable in practice. Short-term rentals are the least tolerated use for carriers. Owners are dropped over aerial-imagery roof photos and then have to prove their case. Yet these homes throw off daily cash flow, and their occupants are unfamiliar visitors with the highest life-safety exposure.
solution: An opt-in $3-6 per night fee at checkout (direct-booking sites and partner property managers) pools into a retrofit financing note for that specific house. Vetted crews install ember-resistant vents, roof and gutter fixes and 5-foot-zone clearing to the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standard. We build a time-stamped evidence pack (photos, receipts, certificate) and file it with the insurer under the new mitigation-credit and dispute rules. Guests see a public 'hardened home' badge. Owner pays nothing up front, and the fee stream repays the financier over 3-5 years.
why_now: Rules now force insurers to credit and explain: Colorado HB25-1182 has applied since 1 July 2026 (score disclosure, documented-mitigation credit, appeal) and California AB 75 (notice, photo copies, remediation window) went operative 1 July 2026. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home just expanded to Washington, signaling national scale. California launched a Safe Homes Grant and a revolving loan program. An FTC all-in-pricing rule for short-term lodging (effective May 2025) makes an opt-in structure the clean design.
revenue_model: 15-20% take of the surcharge flow, financing spread on the retrofit note, 3-5% contractor referral fee, and an insurer or MGA lead fee per credited policy or renewal.
non_obvious_insight: A vacation rental is the rare residential asset with a daily, price-insensitive cash stream that can service a retrofit loan, and guests are exactly the people the hardening protects. That aligns payer and beneficiary. Insurers hate short-term rentals most, so documented hardening changes the underwriting conversation where it matters most.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 owners through Big Bear and Truckee property managers. Get one local roofer or vent installer to give fixed-price bids. Add the opt-in fee line through an existing direct-booking tool (Hospitable, OwnerRez or Lodgify style widgets) and measure guest opt-in rate. Line up a $100-250K revenue-based note from a small local lender or angel. File the first evidence packs with two carriers.

title: Programmable Lockbox for GPU and Robot Collateral
one_liner: Tri-party custody software and hardware that lets lenders verify, and if needed take over, financed GPU clusters and robot fleets sitting in someone else's building.
customer: Specialty and private-credit lenders and equipment lessors financing GPU clouds and robots-as-a-service. Borrowers such as neoclouds and robot operators pay to lower their borrowing spread, and colo operators act as a channel.
problem: More than $20B of loans are now secured by GPUs, and H100-class rental rates fell from about $7-10 per hour in early 2024 to $2-4 by late 2025, so lenders must know whether machines exist, are powered and utilised, and are not double-pledged. Monitoring today is a spreadsheet plus quarterly audits. The bigger trapdoors are the colo landlord's lien for unpaid power or rent and who physically or remotely controls the hardware on default.
solution: (1) A continuous collateral-health feed: hardware serials and attestation (TPM or GPU attestation where available), BMC and out-of-band data, power-meter readings, latency-based geolocation, and periodic photo audits by colo remote hands. (2) Escrowed step-in credentials for BMC and fleet consoles, plus a tri-party lockbox agreement with the colo covering access and lien waivers, with API-triggered 'freeze' and 'transfer to lender' modes. (3) Standard borrowing-base reports.
why_now: GPU-collateralised private credit scaled from almost nothing to over $20B in about two years, with loans maturing 2026-2028 among a small, correlated lender group. Banks avoid the fast-depreciating collateral, leaving private credit to fill the gap. Utilisation and location risk is now board-level for lenders. Robot-as-a-service leasing needs the same control layer.
revenue_model: $15-40 per GPU or robot per month paid by the borrower, or 10-25 bps on outstanding facility size, plus a $25k onboarding fee per facility and colo referral fees.
non_obvious_insight: Lender losses come from control failures such as liens, access and double-pledging, not from chips vanishing. Contracts plus access-control APIs solve most of it. The borrower is the real buyer, because a 50-100 bps lower spread beats the fee, so sell it to the neocloud CFO as a rate reduction.
first_30_days: Speak with 15 specialty lenders and equipment-finance boutiques and 10 GPU-cloud CFOs. Sell a manual 'collateral control audit' at $15-30k for two facilities. Draft the tri-party lockbox template with a finance lawyer, then productise the attestation feed.

title: Advance Hotels Their Stuck OTA Payouts
one_liner: A neutral lender advances 90-95% of completed-stay OTA payouts on checkout day for a flat 1.5-2% fee, so independent hotels stop financing the OTAs.
customer: Independent hotels and small groups of 20-150 rooms in Europe with 60-80% of bookings through Booking.com, Expedia or Agoda.
problem: Insiders treat OTA payment collection as a convenience. In practice about 70% of Booking Holdings' 2025 bookings used its payment service, and hotels are paid after checkout. That is weeks of float while they pay staff, energy and suppliers at costs that have repriced sharply since the Hormuz shock. Banks cannot see these receivables, so nobody underwrites them.
solution: Read reservation and payout schedules from the hotel's channel manager or extranet export. Underwrite each receivable, which is checked out and has a scheduled payout from a top-three OTA. Advance the cash the same day, and sweep repayment when the OTA pays. Later, extend to advances on confirmed future stays for seasonal cash needs.
why_now: OTA merchant payments became the majority path in 2025. Energy and construction costs repriced after the March 2026 Hormuz closure, and capital is described as disciplined and selective. Open banking and embedded-finance rails make small-ticket receivables lending workable for a small team.
revenue_model: A 1.2-2.5% fee per advance, which is about 20-40% annualised on 2-4 week paper, funded by a credit-fund warehouse line, with a small servicing fee.
non_obvious_insight: The merchant model quietly turned hotels into unpriced lenders to OTAs. A checked-out receivable from a top-three OTA is close to risk-free collateral that has never been packaged, because lenders cannot see reservation-level data.
first_30_days: Line up EUR 300-500K from a specialty credit fund or family office. Recruit 5 independent hotels through revenue-management consultants and hotel associations. Offer to advance manually against payout statements they email, testing repayment on the next OTA payout before building any integration.
